claim: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) + palmitic acid (PA) decreased lysosomal Ca2+ ([Ca2+]Lys) in macrophages.
source: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) + palmitic acid (PA) decreased lysosomal Ca2+ ([Ca2+]Lys) and increased [Ca2+]i through mitochondrial ROS, which was suppressed in Trpm2-KO macrophages.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of [Ca2+]Lys using Oregon Green BAPTA-1 Dextran (OGBD) showing significant reduction by LP treatment (Figure 1B).

claim: LPS + PA increased cytosolic Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i) through mitochondrial ROS.
source: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) + palmitic acid (PA) decreased lysosomal Ca2+ ([Ca2+]Lys) and increased [Ca2+]i through mitochondrial ROS, which was suppressed in Trpm2-KO macrophages.
evidence: Supported by Fluo-3-AM and Fura-2 measurements showing significant [Ca2+]i increase by LP (Figure 1C), and suppression by mitochondrial ROS scavenger MitoTEMPOL (Figure 1F).

claim: The LPS + PA-induced increase in [Ca2+]i was suppressed in Trpm2-KO macrophages.
source: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) + palmitic acid (PA) decreased lysosomal Ca2+ ([Ca2+]Lys) and increased [Ca2+]i through mitochondrial ROS, which was suppressed in Trpm2-KO macrophages.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing abrogation of [Ca2+]i increase by LP in Trpm2-KO MΦs (Figure 2A).

claim: Inflammasome activation and metabolic inflammation in adipose tissue of high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice were ameliorated by Trpm2 KO.
source: Inflammasome activation and metabolic inflammation in adipose tissue of high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice were ameliorated by Trpm2 KO.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced ASC specks, caspase-1 cleavage, and crown-like structures in WAT of Trpm2-KO mice on HFD (Figure 3C, D, E).

claim: ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling occurred after lysosomal Ca2+ release.
source: ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling occurred after lysosomal Ca2+ release whose blockade attenuated LPS + PA-induced inflammasome.
evidence: Supported by simultaneous monitoring of [Ca2+]ER and [Ca2+]Lys showing [Ca2+]ER decrease occurring in parallel with [Ca2+]Lys recovery (Figure 4B).

claim: Blockade of ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling attenuated LPS + PA-induced inflammasome.
source: ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling occurred after lysosomal Ca2+ release whose blockade attenuated LPS + PA-induced inflammasome.
evidence: Supported by data showing Xestospongin C (IP3R inhibitor) significantly suppressed IL-1β release by LP (Figure 4D).

claim: Store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE) was activated following ER Ca2+ depletion.
source: Subsequently, store-operated Ca2+entry (SOCE) was activated whose inhibition suppressed inflammasome.
evidence: Supported by STIM1 aggregation and colocalization with ORAI1 after LP treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), and inhibition of inflammasome by SOCE inhibitors BTP2 and 2-APB (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).

claim: Inhibition of SOCE suppressed inflammasome activation.
source: Subsequently, store-operated Ca2+entry (SOCE) was activated whose inhibition suppressed inflammasome.
evidence: Supported by data showing BTP2 and 2-APB significantly reduced IL-1β release by LP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).

claim: SOCE was coupled with K+ efflux.
source: SOCE was coupled with K+ efflux whose inhibition reduced ER Ca2+ content ([Ca2+]ER) and impaired [Ca2+]Lys recovery.
evidence: Supported by data showing high [K+]e significantly reduced [Ca2+]ER by LP (Figure 5A) and suppressed [Ca2+]Lys recovery (Figure 5B).

claim: Inhibition of K+ efflux reduced ER Ca2+ content ([Ca2+]ER).
source: SOCE was coupled with K+ efflux whose inhibition reduced ER Ca2+ content ([Ca2+]ER) and impaired [Ca2+]Lys recovery.
evidence: Supported by data showing high [K+]e significantly reduced [Ca2+]ER by LP (Figure 5A).

claim: Inhibition of K+ efflux impaired [Ca2+]Lys recovery.
source: SOCE was coupled with K+ efflux whose inhibition reduced ER Ca2+ content ([Ca2+]ER) and impaired [Ca2+]Lys recovery.
evidence: Supported by data showing high [K+]e suppressed [Ca2+]Lys recovery after LP removal (Figure 5B).

claim: LPS + PA activated KCa3.1 channel, a Ca2+-activated K+ channel.
source: LPS + PA activated KCa3.1 channel, a Ca2+-activated K+ channel.
evidence: Supported by nystatin-perforated patch clamp data showing increased TRAM-34-sensitive K+ current by LP (Figure 6A, B).

claim: Inhibitors of KCa3.1 channel reduced [Ca2+]ER.
source: Inhibitors of KCa3.1 channel or Kcnn4 KO reduced [Ca2+]ER, attenuated increase of [Ca2+]i or inflammasome activation by LPS + PA, and ameliorated HFD-induced inflammasome or metabolic inflammation.
evidence: Supported by data showing TRAM-34 significantly reduced [Ca2+]ER by LP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Inhibitors of KCa3.1 channel attenuated increase of [Ca2+]i by LPS + PA.
source: Inhibitors of KCa3.1 channel or Kcnn4 KO reduced [Ca2+]ER, attenuated increase of [Ca2+]i or inflammasome activation by LPS + PA, and ameliorated HFD-induced inflammasome or metabolic inflammation.
evidence: Supported by data showing TRAM-34 inhibited [Ca2+]i increase by LP (Figure 5D).

claim: Inhibitors of KCa3.1 channel attenuated inflammasome activation by LPS + PA.
source: Inhibitors of KCa3.1 channel or Kcnn4 KO reduced [Ca2+]ER, attenuated increase of [Ca2+]i or inflammasome activation by LPS + PA, and ameliorated HFD-induced inflammasome or metabolic inflammation.
evidence: Supported by data showing TRAM-34 significantly decreased IL-1β release by LP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).

claim: Kcnn4 KO reduced [Ca2+]ER.
source: Inhibitors of KCa3.1 channel or Kcnn4 KO reduced [Ca2+]ER, attenuated increase of [Ca2+]i or inflammasome activation by LPS + PA, and ameliorated HFD-induced inflammasome or metabolic inflammation.
evidence: Inferred from the coupling between K+ efflux and SOCE, and data showing Kcnn4 KO abrogated [K+]i decrease by LP (Figure 6F).

claim: Kcnn4 KO attenuated inflammasome activation by LPS + PA.
source: Inhibitors of KCa3.1 channel or Kcnn4 KO reduced [Ca2+]ER, attenuated increase of [Ca2+]i or inflammasome activation by LPS + PA, and ameliorated HFD-induced inflammasome or metabolic inflammation.
evidence: Supported by data showing IL-1β release and inflammasome activation by LP were significantly reduced by Kcnn4 KO (Figure 6E).

claim: Kcnn4 KO ameliorated HFD-induced inflammasome.
source: Inhibitors of KCa3.1 channel or Kcnn4 KO reduced [Ca2+]ER, attenuated increase of [Ca2+]i or inflammasome activation by LPS + PA, and ameliorated HFD-induced inflammasome or metabolic inflammation.
evidence: Supported by data showing attenuated caspase-1 cleavage and significantly reduced ASC specks in WAT of Kcnn4-KO mice on HFD (Figure 6I, J).

claim: Kcnn4 KO ameliorated HFD-induced metabolic inflammation.
source: Inhibitors of KCa3.1 channel or Kcnn4 KO reduced [Ca2+]ER, attenuated increase of [Ca2+]i or inflammasome activation by LPS + PA, and ameliorated HFD-induced inflammasome or metabolic inflammation.
evidence: Supported by data showing significantly reduced crown-like structures in WAT and improved glucose tolerance in Kcnn4-KO mice on HFD (Figure 6K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).

claim: Lysosomal Ca2+ release induced delayed JNK activation through CAMKII-ASK1.
source: Lysosomal Ca2+ release induced delayed JNK and ASC phosphorylation through CAMKII-ASK1.
evidence: Supported by data showing JNK activation by LP at 21 hr (Figure 7A), inhibition by KN-93 (CaMKII inhibitor) and selonsertib (ASK1 inhibitor) (Figure 7F, 7E), and suppression by Kcnn4 or Trpm2 KO (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Lysosomal Ca2+ release induced delayed ASC phosphorylation through CAMKII-ASK1.
source: Lysosomal Ca2+ release induced delayed JNK and ASC phosphorylation through CAMKII-ASK1.
evidence: Supported by data showing ASC phosphorylation occurred 21 hr after LP treatment (Figure 7B), and was inhibited by KN-93 and selonsertib (Figure 7D).

claim: Perilysosomal Ca2+ release by GPN was significantly reduced after LP treatment.
source: When we studied perilysosomal Ca2+ release in bone marrow-derived macrophages (MΦs) (BMDMs) transfected with GCaMP3-ML1 (Shen et al., 2012), lysosomal Ca2+ release was not directly visualized by LP; however, perilysosomal Ca2+ release by Gly-Phe β-naphthylamide (GPN), a lysosomotropic agent (Shen et al., 2012), was significantly reduced (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1), suggesting preemptying or release of lysosomal Ca2+ by LP, similar to the results using other inducers of lysosomal Ca2+ release (Park et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by GCaMP3-ML1 fluorescence measurements showing reduced peak fluorescence after GPN application in LP-treated cells (Figure 1A).

claim: Reduced perilysosomal Ca2+ release by GPN after LP treatment suggests preemptying or release of lysosomal Ca2+ by LP.
source: When we studied perilysosomal Ca2+ release in bone marrow-derived macrophages (MΦs) (BMDMs) transfected with GCaMP3-ML1 (Shen et al., 2012), lysosomal Ca2+ release was not directly visualized by LP; however, perilysosomal Ca2+ release by Gly-Phe β-naphthylamide (GPN), a lysosomotropic agent (Shen et al., 2012), was significantly reduced (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1), suggesting preemptying or release of lysosomal Ca2+ by LP, similar to the results using other inducers of lysosomal Ca2+ release (Park et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GPN-induced perilysosomal Ca2+ release was reduced after LP treatment, and supported by citations to similar findings with other lysosomal Ca2+ release inducers.

claim: BAPTA-AM abrogated IL-1β release by LP.
source: Functional roles of increased [Ca2+]i in inflammasome by LP were revealed by abrogation of IL-1β release or IL-1β maturation by BAPTA-AM, a cell-permeable Ca2+ chelator (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing BAPTA-AM significantly reduced IL-1β release by LP (Figure 1D).

claim: BAPTA-AM abrogated IL-1β maturation by LP.
source: Functional roles of increased [Ca2+]i in inflammasome by LP were revealed by abrogation of IL-1β release or IL-1β maturation by BAPTA-AM, a cell-permeable Ca2+ chelator (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing BAPTA-AM reduced mature IL-1β (Figure 1E).

claim: Pro-IL-1β level was not notably affected by BAPTA-AM.
source: Immunoblotting (IB) demonstrated that pro-IL-1β level was not notably affected by BAPTA-AM, suggesting that the effect of BAPTA-AM was unrelated to the potential inhibition of pro-IL-1β transcription or translation (Figure 1E, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing similar pro-IL-1β levels with and without BAPTA-AM (Figure 1E).

claim: The effect of BAPTA-AM was unrelated to the potential inhibition of pro-IL-1β transcription or translation.
source: Immunoblotting (IB) demonstrated that pro-IL-1β level was not notably affected by BAPTA-AM, suggesting that the effect of BAPTA-AM was unrelated to the potential inhibition of pro-IL-1β transcription or translation (Figure 1E, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pro-IL-1β levels were unchanged by BAPTA-AM.

claim: LP effectively induced ROS accumulation.
source: LP effectively induced CM-H2DCFDA fluorescence indicating ROS accumulation, while PA alone or LPS alone induced only a little ROS accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting synergistic effect of LPS and PA.
evidence: Supported by CM-H2DCFDA fluorescence measurements showing significantly higher ROS in LP-treated cells compared to PA or LPS alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: PA alone or LPS alone induced only a little ROS accumulation.
source: LP effectively induced CM-H2DCFDA fluorescence indicating ROS accumulation, while PA alone or LPS alone induced only a little ROS accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting synergistic effect of LPS and PA.
evidence: Supported by CM-H2DCFDA fluorescence measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: LPS and PA have a synergistic effect on ROS accumulation.
source: LP effectively induced CM-H2DCFDA fluorescence indicating ROS accumulation, while PA alone or LPS alone induced only a little ROS accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting synergistic effect of LPS and PA.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that LP induced much more ROS than PA or LPS alone.

claim: NAC abrogated release and maturation of IL-1β by LP.
source: When we studied the roles of ROS in [Ca2+]i increase using N-acetyl cysteine (NAC), an antioxidant (Tardiolo et al., 2018), release and maturation of IL-1β by LP were significantly reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 1E, Figure 1—source data 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by ELISA and immunoblotting data showing NAC significantly reduced IL-1β release and maturation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 1E).

claim: NAC abrogated LP-induced increase of [Ca2+]i.
source: NAC abrogated LP-induced increase of [Ca2+]i as well (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1), substantiating the functional roles of ROS in [Ca2+]i increase and inflammasome activation.
evidence: Supported by Fluo-3-AM and Fura-2 measurements showing NAC prevented [Ca2+]i increase by LP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: LP induced significant mitochondrial ROS accumulation.
source: Using MitoSOX, we observed significant mitochondrial ROS accumulation by LP.
evidence: Supported by MitoSOX staining and flow cytometry data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: MitoTEMPOL quenched mitochondrial ROS.
source: When we quenched mitochondrial ROS using MitoTEMPOL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1), IL-1β release by LP was significantly reduced (Figure 1F, Figure 1—source data 1), suggesting crucial roles of mitochondrial ROS in LP-induced inflammasome.
evidence: Supported by MitoSOX data showing MitoTEMPOL reduced mitochondrial ROS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: MitoTEMPOL significantly reduced IL-1β release by LP.
source: When we quenched mitochondrial ROS using MitoTEMPOL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1), IL-1β release by LP was significantly reduced (Figure 1F, Figure 1—source data 1), suggesting crucial roles of mitochondrial ROS in LP-induced inflammasome.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing MitoTEMPOL significantly reduced IL-1β release (Figure 1F).

claim: Mitochondrial ROS plays crucial roles in LP-induced inflammasome.
source: When we quenched mitochondrial ROS using MitoTEMPOL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1), IL-1β release by LP was significantly reduced (Figure 1F, Figure 1—source data 1), suggesting crucial roles of mitochondrial ROS in LP-induced inflammasome.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that quenching mitochondrial ROS with MitoTEMPOL significantly reduced inflammasome activation.

claim: TRPM2 is expressed on lysosomes of BMDMs.
source: We verified the expression of TRPM2 on lysosome of BMDMs by colocalization of TRPM2 and LAMP2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing colocalization of TRPM2 and LAMP2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: ROS can activate TRPM2 by increasing ADPR production from poly-ADPR.
source: While the physiological ligand of TRPM2 is ADP-ribose (ADPR), ROS can activate TRPM2 by increasing ADPR production from poly-ADPR (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Apigenin significantly inhibited inflammasome by LP.
source: Inflammasome by LP was significantly inhibited by apigenin or quercetin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting that TRPM2 participates in inflammasome by LP.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing apigenin reduced IL-1β release by LP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Quercetin significantly inhibited inflammasome by LP.
source: Inflammasome by LP was significantly inhibited by apigenin or quercetin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting that TRPM2 participates in inflammasome by LP.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing quercetin reduced IL-1β release by LP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: TRPM2 participates in inflammasome by LP.
source: Inflammasome by LP was significantly inhibited by apigenin or quercetin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting that TRPM2 participates in inflammasome by LP.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD38 inhibitors (apigenin, quercetin) that block ADPR generation inhibited inflammasome.

claim: Apigenin reduced [Ca2+]i increase by LP.
source: [Ca2+]i increase by LP was also reduced by apigenin or quercetin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1), supporting that apigenin or quercetin suppresses inflammasome through the inhibition of lysosomal Ca2+ channels activated by ADPR such as TRPM2.
evidence: Supported by Fluo-3-AM and Fura-2 measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Quercetin reduced [Ca2+]i increase by LP.
source: [Ca2+]i increase by LP was also reduced by apigenin or quercetin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1), supporting that apigenin or quercetin suppresses inflammasome through the inhibition of lysosomal Ca2+ channels activated by ADPR such as TRPM2.
evidence: Supported by Fluo-3-AM and Fura-2 measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Apigenin or quercetin suppresses inflammasome through the inhibition of lysosomal Ca2+ channels activated by ADPR such as TRPM2.
source: [Ca2+]i increase by LP was also reduced by apigenin or quercetin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1), supporting that apigenin or quercetin suppresses inflammasome through the inhibition of lysosomal Ca2+ channels activated by ADPR such as TRPM2.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD38 inhibitors reduced both [Ca2+]i and inflammasome activation.

claim: [Ca2+]i increase by LP was abrogated in Trpm2-KO MΦs.
source: [Ca2+]i increase and [Ca2+]Lys decrease by LP were abrogated in Trpm2-KO MΦs (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—source data 1), suggesting the roles of TRPM2 in lysosomal Ca2+ release by LP.
evidence: Supported by Fluo-3-AM and Fura-2 measurements showing no [Ca2+]i increase in Trpm2-KO cells treated with LP (Figure 2A).

claim: [Ca2+]Lys decrease by LP was abrogated in Trpm2-KO MΦs.
source: [Ca2+]i increase and [Ca2+]Lys decrease by LP were abrogated in Trpm2-KO MΦs (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—source data 1), suggesting the roles of TRPM2 in lysosomal Ca2+ release by LP.
evidence: Supported by OGBD measurements showing no [Ca2+]Lys decrease in Trpm2-KO cells treated with LP (Figure 2B).

claim: TRPM2 plays a role in lysosomal Ca2+ release by LP.
source: [Ca2+]i increase and [Ca2+]Lys decrease by LP were abrogated in Trpm2-KO MΦs (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—source data 1), suggesting the roles of TRPM2 in lysosomal Ca2+ release by LP.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Trpm2 KO prevented both [Ca2+]i increase and [Ca2+]Lys decrease by LP.

claim: ROS production by LP was not changed by Trpm2 KO.
source: However, ROS production by LP was not changed by Trpm2 KO (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting that TRPM2 is downstream of ROS.
evidence: Supported by CM-H2DCFDA fluorescence measurements showing similar ROS levels in Trpm2+/+ and Trpm2-/- cells treated with LP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claim: TRPM2 is downstream of ROS.
source: However, ROS production by LP was not changed by Trpm2 KO (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting that TRPM2 is downstream of ROS.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Trpm2 KO did not affect ROS production.

claim: Inflammasome activation by LP was significantly reduced by Trpm2 KO.
source: Importantly, inflammasome activation assessed by IL-1β ELISA of culture supernatant or IB of peritoneal MΦ lysate after LP treatment was significantly reduced by Trpm2 KO (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2), indicating the roles of TRPM2, likely lysosomal TRPM2, in inflammasome by LP.
evidence: Supported by ELISA and immunoblotting data showing reduced IL-1β release and caspase-1 cleavage in Trpm2-KO cells (Figure 2C).

claim: TRPM2, likely lysosomal TRPM2, plays a role in inflammasome by LP.
source: Importantly, inflammasome activation assessed by IL-1β ELISA of culture supernatant or IB of peritoneal MΦ lysate after LP treatment was significantly reduced by Trpm2 KO (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2), indicating the roles of TRPM2, likely lysosomal TRPM2, in inflammasome by LP.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Trpm2 KO reduced inflammasome activation, combined with evidence of lysosomal TRPM2 expression.

claim: ASC speck formation by LP was markedly reduced by Trpm2 KO.
source: ASC speck formation, a marker of inflammasome, by LP was also markedly reduced by Trpm2 KO (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing significantly fewer ASC specks in Trpm2-KO cells treated with LP (Figure 2D).

claim: Inflammasome activation by LLOMe was significantly inhibited by Trpm2 KO.
source: When we employed other activators, inflammasome activation by L-Leucyl-L-Leucine methyl ester (LLOMe) or monosodium urate (MSU), lysosomotropic agents, was significantly inhibited by Trpm2 KO.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing reduced IL-1β release by LLOMe in Trpm2-KO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Inflammasome activation by MSU was significantly inhibited by Trpm2 KO.
source: When we employed other activators, inflammasome activation by L-Leucyl-L-Leucine methyl ester (LLOMe) or monosodium urate (MSU), lysosomotropic agents, was significantly inhibited by Trpm2 KO.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing reduced IL-1β release by MSU in Trpm2-KO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Inflammasome by nigericin was not significantly affected by Trpm2 KO.
source: However, inflammasome by nigericin, an ionophore exchanging K+ for H+ or ATP acting on P2X7 ion channel on the plasma membrane (Campden and Zhang, 2019), was not significantly affected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting that TRPM2 channel is crucial in inflammasome involving lysosomal Ca2+.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing similar IL-1β release by nigericin in Trpm2+/+ and Trpm2-/- cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Inflammasome by ATP was not significantly affected by Trpm2 KO.
source: However, inflammasome by nigericin, an ionophore exchanging K+ for H+ or ATP acting on P2X7 ion channel on the plasma membrane (Campden and Zhang, 2019), was not significantly affected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting that TRPM2 channel is crucial in inflammasome involving lysosomal Ca2+.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing similar IL-1β release by ATP in Trpm2+/+ and Trpm2-/- cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: TRPM2 channel is crucial in inflammasome involving lysosomal Ca2+.
source: However, inflammasome by nigericin, an ionophore exchanging K+ for H+ or ATP acting on P2X7 ion channel on the plasma membrane (Campden and Zhang, 2019), was not significantly affected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting that TRPM2 channel is crucial in inflammasome involving lysosomal Ca2+.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Trpm2 KO inhibited inflammasome by lysosomotropic agents but not by nigericin or ATP which act on plasma membrane channels.

claim: Nonfasting blood glucose was significantly lower in Trpm2-KO mice on HFD compared to control mice on HFD.
source: Nonfasting blood glucose was significantly lower in Trpm2-KO mice on high-fat diet (HFD) compared to control mice on HFD (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1), while body weight was not different between them (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurements showing significantly lower glucose in Trpm2-KO mice on HFD (Figure 3A).

claim: Body weight was not different between Trpm2+/+ and Trpm2-/- mice on HFD.
source: Nonfasting blood glucose was significantly lower in Trpm2-KO mice on high-fat diet (HFD) compared to control mice on HFD (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1), while body weight was not different between them (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements showing no significant difference (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Trpm2-KO mice on HFD showed significantly ameliorated glucose intolerance.
source: Intraperitoneal glucose tolerance test (IPGTT) showed significantly ameliorated glucose intolerance and reduced area under the curve (AUC) in Trpm2-KO mice on HFD (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by IPGTT data showing improved glucose tolerance in Trpm2-KO mice on HFD (Figure 3B).

claim: Trpm2-KO mice on HFD showed reduced area under the curve (AUC) in IPGTT.
source: Intraperitoneal glucose tolerance test (IPGTT) showed significantly ameliorated glucose intolerance and reduced area under the curve (AUC) in Trpm2-KO mice on HFD (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by AUC calculations from IPGTT data (Figure 3B).

claim: HOMA-IR was significantly reduced in Trpm2-KO mice on HFD.
source: HOMA-IR, an index of insulin resistance, was also significantly reduced in Trpm2-KO mice on HFD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by HOMA-IR calculations showing significantly lower values in Trpm2-KO mice on HFD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: The number of crown-like structures (CLS) was significantly reduced in WAT of Trpm2-KO mice on HFD.
source: The number of crown-like structures (CLS) representing metabolic inflammation (Weisberg et al., 2003) was significantly reduced in while adipose tissue (WAT) of Trpm2-KO mice on HFD (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1), suggesting reduced metabolic inflammation by Trpm2 KO.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis showing significantly fewer CLS in Trpm2-KO mice on HFD (Figure 3C).

claim: Trpm2 KO reduced metabolic inflammation.
source: The number of crown-like structures (CLS) representing metabolic inflammation (Weisberg et al., 2003) was significantly reduced in while adipose tissue (WAT) of Trpm2-KO mice on HFD (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1), suggesting reduced metabolic inflammation by Trpm2 KO.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CLS, a marker of metabolic inflammation, were reduced in Trpm2-KO mice.

claim: The number of ASC specks was significantly reduced in WAT of Trpm2-KO mice on HFD.
source: Inflammasome activation was also significantly reduced in WAT of Trpm2-KO mice on HFD as evidenced by the significantly reduced numbers of ASC specks and capase-1 cleavage (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2), indicating that TRPM2 is important in inflammasome related to metabolic syndrome.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing significantly fewer ASC specks in Trpm2-KO mice on HFD (Figure 3D).

claim: Caspase-1 cleavage was significantly reduced in WAT of Trpm2-KO mice on HFD.
source: Inflammasome activation was also significantly reduced in WAT of Trpm2-KO mice on HFD as evidenced by the significantly reduced numbers of ASC specks and capase-1 cleavage (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2), indicating that TRPM2 is important in inflammasome related to metabolic syndrome.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing reduced caspase-1 p20 in Trpm2-KO mice on HFD (Figure 3E).

claim: TRPM2 is important in inflammasome related to metabolic syndrome.
source: Inflammasome activation was also significantly reduced in WAT of Trpm2-KO mice on HFD as evidenced by the significantly reduced numbers of ASC specks and capase-1 cleavage (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2), indicating that TRPM2 is important in inflammasome related to metabolic syndrome.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Trpm2 KO reduced inflammasome activation and metabolic inflammation in HFD-fed mice.

claim: ACA inhibited IL-1β release by LP.
source: ACA could inhibit IL-1β release by LP as expected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing ACA reduced IL-1β release by LP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Intracellular dialysis using cyclic ADPR induced slow inward current on the plasma membrane.
source: Intracellular dialysis using cyclic ADPR induced slow inward current on the plasma membrane, which was inhibited by ACA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp data showing inward current development with cyclic ADPR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Cyclic ADPR-induced inward current was inhibited by ACA.
source: Intracellular dialysis using cyclic ADPR induced slow inward current on the plasma membrane, which was inhibited by ACA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp data showing ACA inhibited the inward current (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The amplitude of cyclic ADPR-induced inward current was not affected by PA and/or LPS.
source: The amplitude of cyclic ADPR-induced inward current was not affected by PA and/or LPS (b–c in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by patch clamp data showing similar current amplitudes across treatment groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).

claim: Basal inward current inhibited by ACA was not changed by PA and/or LPS.

claim: [Ca2+]ER decrease occurred in parallel with [Ca2+]Lys recovery.

evidence: Supported by simultaneous monitoring showing inverse relationship between [Ca2+]ER and [Ca2+]Lys (Figure 4B).

claim: ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling occurs during lysosomal Ca2+ recovery.

evidence: Inferred from the observation that [Ca2+]ER decreased as [Ca2+]Lys increased after LP removal.

claim: Xestospongin C inhibited recovery of [Ca2+]Lys after LP removal.

claim: Dantrolene did not significantly affect recovery of [Ca2+]Lys.

claim: TPEN markedly inhibited recovery of [Ca2+]Lys after LP removal.

evidence: Supported by OGBD measurements showing TPEN prevented [Ca2+]Lys recovery (Figure 4C).

claim: ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling occurs during lysosomal Ca2+ recovery.
source: When we chelated ER Ca2+ with a membrane-permeant metal chelator N,N,N',N'-tetrakis (2-pyridylmethyl)ethylene diamine (TPEN) that has a low Ca2+ affinity and can chelate ER Ca2+ but not cytosolic Ca2+ (Hofer et al., 1998), recovery of [Ca2+]Lys after LP removal was markedly inhibited (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 1), again supporting ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling during lysosomal Ca2 recovery.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that chelating ER Ca2+ prevented lysosomal Ca2+ recovery.

claim: Xestospongin C significantly suppressed IL-1β release by LP.

evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing Xestospongin C reduced IL-1β release by LP (Figure 4D).

claim: ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling contributes to inflammasome by LP.

evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling with Xestospongin C reduced inflammasome activation.

claim: LP induced multiple contacts between VAPA on ER and ORP1L on lysosome.

claim: Organelle contact facilitates ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling.

evidence: Inferred from the observation that ER-lysosome contacts increased during ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling, and supported by citation to Yang et al., 2019.

evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing EGTA reduced IL-1β release by LP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Extracellular Ca2+ plays a role in inflammasome by LP.
source: When extracellular Ca2+ was chelated by 3 mM EGTA reducing [Ca2+]i in RPMI medium to 99 nM (Schoenmakers et al., 1992) below [Ca2+]i in Ca2+-free medium (Maggi et al., 1989), IL-1β release by LP was significantly reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1), demonstrating the roles of extracellular Ca2+ in inflammasome by LP.

claim: BTP2 significantly reduced IL-1β release by LP.

claim: STIM1 aggregation was clearly observed after LP treatment.

evidence: Supported by D1ER measurements showing [Ca2+]ER reduction by LP at high [K+]e (Figure 5A).

claim: K+ efflux is coupled to extracellular Ca2+ influx through SOCE.

source: [Ca2+]Lys recovery after LP removal became significantly lower by high [K+]e (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting that high [K+]e dampens [Ca2+]Lys recovery after LP removal likely through SOCE inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that high [K+]e, which inhibits K+ efflux and thus SOCE, reduced [Ca2+]Lys recovery.

evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing no significant effect of quinine on IL-1β release by LP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Barium sulfate did not significantly inhibit IL-1β release by LP.

claim: JNK was activated by LP treatment for 21 hr.
source: JNK was activated by LP treatment for 21 hr (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing JNK phosphorylation after LP treatment for 21 hr (Figure 7A).

claim: JNK activation by LPS alone occurred 30 min after treatment and subsided since 2 hr.
source: JNK activation by LPS alone occurred 30 min after treatment, subsided since 2 hr, and never occurred again (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by time-course immunoblotting data showing transient JNK phosphorylation after LPS treatment (Figure 7A).

evidence: Supported by Fluo-3-AM measurements showing higher [Ca2+]i at 21 hr compared to 4 hr after LP treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Ca2+ influx supported by K+ efflux is pronounced at later time of LP treatment.

evidence: Inferred from the observation that K+ efflux occurred at later time points.

evidence: Inferred from the observation that ER Ca2+ depletion occurred at later time points.

evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing ASC phosphorylation at 21 hr after LP but not at 0.5 hr after LPS (Figure 7B).

evidence: Supported by DSS crosslinking and immunoblotting data showing ASC oligomers at 21 hr after LP but not at 0.5 hr after LPS (Figure 7C).

evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing reduced JNK phosphorylation in Trpm2-KO cells treated with LP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Events such as lysosomal Ca2+ release and/or K+ efflux are necessary for delayed JNK activation.

claim: SP600125 suppressed ASC phosphorylation by LP.
source: SP600125, a JNK inhibitor, suppressed ASC phosphorylation and oligomerization by LP (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 2), indicating that JNK activation is necessary but not sufficient for ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization, as shown by no ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization 0.5 hr after LPS treatment despite strong JNK activation (Figure 7B and C, Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing SP600125 reduced ASC phosphorylation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).

claim: SP600125 suppressed ASC oligomerization by LP.

evidence: Supported by DSS crosslinking and immunoblotting data showing SP600125 reduced ASC oligomers (Figure 7D).

claim: JNK activation is necessary but not sufficient for ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization.
source: SP600125, a JNK inhibitor, suppressed ASC phosphorylation and oligomerization by LP (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 2), indicating that JNK activation is necessary but not sufficient for ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization, as shown by no ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization 0.5 hr after LPS treatment despite strong JNK activation (Figure 7B and C, Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that JNK inhibitor blocked ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization, and that JNK activation alone (at 0.5 hr after LPS) did not induce ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization.

claim: IL-1β release by LP was inhibited by JNK inhibitor.

evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing SP600125 reduced IL-1β release by LP (Figure 7E).

claim: IL-1β release by LP was not inhibited by 5Z-7-oxozeaenol, a TAK1 inhibitor.

evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing no significant effect of 5Z-7-oxozeaenol on IL-1β release by LP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Activated ASK1 induces JNK activation and subsequent ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization.

evidence: Inferred from the observation that ASK1 inhibitor blocked both JNK activation and ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization.

claim: ASK1 activation by LP was attenuated by KN-93, a CaMKII inhibitor.
source: When we studied the mechanism of ASK1 activation by LP, ASK1 activation by LP was attenuated by KN-93, a CaMKII inhibitor, but not by KN-92, a KN-93 congener without CaMKII inhibitory activity (Figure 7F, Figure 7—source data 2), which supports the roles of increased [Ca2+]i and subsequent CAMKII in ASK1 activation by LP, similar to the inhibition of lysosomal rupture-induced inflammasome by KN-93 (Okada et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing KN-93 reduced ASK1 phosphorylation (Figure 7F).

claim: ASK1 activation by LP was not attenuated by KN-92.
source: When we studied the mechanism of ASK1 activation by LP, ASK1 activation by LP was attenuated by KN-93, a CaMKII inhibitor, but not by KN-92, a KN-93 congener without CaMKII inhibitory activity (Figure 7F, Figure 7—source data 2), which supports the roles of increased [Ca2+]i and subsequent CAMKII in ASK1 activation by LP, similar to the inhibition of lysosomal rupture-induced inflammasome by KN-93 (Okada et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing KN-92 did not reduce ASK1 phosphorylation (Figure 7F).

claim: Increased [Ca2+]i and subsequent CAMKII play roles in ASK1 activation by LP.

evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing KN-93 but not KN-92 reduced JNK phosphorylation (Figure 7F).

claim: IL-1β maturation by LP was inhibited by KN-93 but not by KN-92.
source: JNK phosphorylation and inflammasome activation as evidenced by maturation or release of IL-1β by LP were also inhibited by KN-93 but not by KN-92 (Figure 7F–H, Figure 7—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing KN-93 but not KN-92 reduced mature IL-1β (Figure 7G).

claim: IL-1β release by LP was inhibited by KN-93 but not by KN-92.
source: JNK phosphorylation and inflammasome activation as evidenced by maturation or release of IL-1β by LP were also inhibited by KN-93 but not by KN-92 (Figure 7F–H, Figure 7—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing KN-93 but not KN-92 reduced IL-1β release (Figure 7H).

claim: Increased [Ca2+]i due to lysosomal Ca2+ release facilitated by ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling and K+ efflux through KCa3.1 channel induces delayed activation of ASK1 and JNK, leading to ASC oligomerization or NLRP3 inflammasome by LP and metabolic inflammation.
source: These results indicate that increased [Ca2+]i due to lysosomal Ca2+ release facilitated by ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling and K+ efflux through KCa3.1 channel induces delayed activation of ASK1 and JNK, leading to ASC oligomerization or NLRP3 inflammasome by LP and metabolic inflammation.
evidence: Inferred from the collective observations of lysosomal Ca2+ release, ER→lysosome refilling, K+ efflux through KCa3.1, CaMKII-ASK1-JNK pathway activation, and ASC oligomerization.
